nodes.question: How does the article suggest farmer decisions impact harvested area variations?
nodes.answer: The article suggests that farmer decisions based on economic factors significantly influence variations in harvested area.
nodes.paragraph: Article https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-25-57420-6 Swapping rice for alternative cereals can reduce climate-induced production lossesand increase farmer incomes in India Dongyang Wei1,2, Leslie Guadalupe Castro3, Ashwini Chhatre4, Marta Tuninetti5& Kyle Frankel Davis1,6 The rising homogeneity of global crop supply has increased vulnerability to climatic and economic disruptions. Whil e substantial work has examined yield variations in relation to climate variability, little is known about the in uence of harvested area on production stability . To investigate this, here we take the example of monsoon cereal production in India, which has steadily shifted towards climate-sensitive rice an d away from alternative cereals ( nger millet, maize, pearl millet, and sorghum). We nd that variations in harvested area are signi cantly associated with current and past price uctuations for all cereals except rice. This suggests that farme r decisions based on economic factors may exercise great in uence in determining variations in harvested area. We also show that optimized allocations of harvested area can reduce climate- induced production loss by 11% or improve farmer net pro t by 11% while maintaining calorie production and cro pland area.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Climate-resilient agriculture practices_qna_001
nodes.label: Experimental design and 15N application
nodes.question: What types of plots were established for the crop experiments?
nodes.answer: Six macroplots were established, which included mesoplots (1.4 m x 1.4 m) and microplots (30 cm x 30 cm) within each macroplot.
nodes.paragraph: Experimental design and 15N application For each crop, 6 macroplots (WW: 3 m 8 m, SB: 3 m 11 m) were defined. Within each macroplot, a mes- oplot (1.4 m 1.4 m) and a microplot ( 30 cm) were established (Supplementary Fig. S1). In the mesoplots, we applied low 15N enrichment labeling (~ 5 at%) to determine fertilizer-derived plant N uptake and to trace translocation of fertilizer N in soil. The microplots were fertilized with high 15N enrichment (~ 60 at%) and used for gas sampling. For WW, microplots were chosen where uniformly grow - ing plants were present, for SB one representative plant was identified. Meso- and microplots remained at the same spot throughout the growing seasons. Both crops were fertilized according to their N demand and yield potential, typical for these crops in the region. WW was fertilized with 21 g N m 2 (equivalent to 210 kg N ha 1) split in two fertilizer doses of 14 g N m 2 on April 8th and 7 g N m 2 on June 11th.

nodes.question: What factors influence the properties and distribution of I. griffithii?
nodes.answer: The properties and distribution of I. griffithii are influenced by geographic location, climate, and soil conditions.

The properties and distribution of I. griffithii are influenced by a range of environmental factors, including geographic location, climate, and soil conditions6,7. Climate change, along with habitat modification and degradation, significantly contributes to the rarity of specific species and the decline of biodiversity. Recent studies have extensively studied the impact of climate on distribution of plant species. Climate change can alter the species distribution which results in range shifts, habitat fragmentation and extinction of species. The studies carried out in species like Magnolia wufengensis8, Polygonum capitatum9, and Tecomella undulata10 indicate a drastic fluctuation in their suitable habitats due to temperature and precipitation changes. In this regard, different modeling approaches are beneficial for simulating a range of potential outcomes for target species, supporting decision-makers in minimizing biological consequences and preparing for possible changes. Species distribution models (SDMs) are most widely used to identify the environmental predictors that determine habitats suitability and to predict the impacts of climate change on various biota8.

nodes.paragraph: (iii) Further, we aimed at generating a full dataset to be used for optimization and validation of N2 fluxes in modelling as proposed by Grosz et al. (2021). We hypothesized, that growth and development patterns of different plant species control all drivers of denitrification (O2, NO3 , and Corg availability, temperature) and therefore N2O, and N2 losses and N2O/(N2O + N2) ratios. In detail, we expect that (1) plant N uptake governs NO3 availability for denitrification leading to higher N2O and N2 emissions when plant N uptake is low. (2) Increasing C availability increases denitrification derived N losses and decreases the N2O/(N2O + N2) ratio. And (3) denitrification-promoting effects of Corg supply to soil by rhizodeposition are inferior to denitrification-lowering effects caused by plant uptake of NO3 and water. Methods Study site and crop management The experiment was conducted on the experimental farm Reinshof of the Georg-August University G ttingen, Germany (51.499 N, 9.931 E, 157 m a.s.l.) during 2021. The mean annual temperature of the area is 9.3 C and the mean annual precipitation is 628 mm (30-year mean, 1992 to 2021, (DWD 2021)).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Climate-resilient agriculture practices_qna_004
nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What are some recommended adaptation strategies for cocoa farming in Ekiti State?
nodes.answer: Recommended strategies include microclimate protection, farm diversification, adoption of heat and drought-resistant crops, and improved farm management.
nodes.paragraph: 2021). As a largely smallholder-grown crop, cocoa is also important for livelihoods and local land management, lending it strong social and cultural significance (Adejare 2021). In 2020, Ekiti State produced nearly 8,0 tonnes of graded cocoa (Ekiti State Government 2021a). Ekiti State together with Ogun, Ondo, Osun, and Edo states produces 80% of Nigeria S cocoa output (Awoy - emi and Aderinoye-Abdulwahab 2019). Predicted cli- matic changes are likely to decrease the suitability of Ekiti State for cocoa farming by 10 20% by 2050 (Schroth et al. 2016). Without adoption of appropri- ate adaptation measures, the future viability of the cocoa sector in Ekiti State could be at risk. Recom- mended climate adaptation strategies for cocoa in the region include microclimate protection (e.g., through shading), farm diversification, adoption of heat and drought-resistant crops, and improved farm manage- ment (Schroth et al. 2017). Nigeria S and Ekiti State S plans for agricultural development and cocoa revitalization historically encouraged land clearing and industrialization to maximize short-term returns (Ojong and Anam 2018; Lokpobiri 2019; Ekiti State Government 2020a, b).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Climate-resilient agriculture practices_qna_005
nodes.question: Why is the adjustment of practice management measures necessary in response to new environmental challenges?
nodes.answer: The adjustment of practice management measures is necessary to manage new environmental challenges as future climate changes are expected to further amplify existing climate-related risks and create new ones, such as soil degradation and environmental pollution.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Climate-resilient agriculture practices_qna_006
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How can wine-growers adapt to the new climatic conditions caused by global warming?
nodes.answer: Wine-growers can adapt to the new climatic conditions by cultivating other varieties that are better suited to the new conditions, which could help reduce the loss of cultivation areas.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Climate-resilient agriculture practices_qna_007
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What is the primary basis for climate models focused on the future of vine growing?
nodes.answer: Climate models focused on the future of vine growing are primarily based on the Dublin index, which utilizes daily average and maximum temperatures during the growing season.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Climate-resilient agriculture practices_qna_008
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How many climate models are currently in use for predicting the future of vine growing?
nodes.answer: There are around 40 climate models from various world institutions being used, with five selected for analysis, including CNRM from France and Had GEM from England.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Climate-resilient agriculture practices_qna_009
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How do the major climatological models predict the cultivation of specific vine varieties of the Czech Republic throughout the 21st century?
nodes.answer: The major climatological models (BNU, CNRM, Had GEM, IPS, and MRI) provide predictions for the cultivation of vine varieties of the Czech Republic during different periods of the 21st century, with each model offering two variants for the same time frame.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Climate-resilient agriculture practices_qna_010
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How can winegrowers adjust various parameters to combat rising temperatures during the ripening phase of grape cultivation?
nodes.answer: Winegrowers can adjust various parameters by selecting heat and drought-resistant wine varieties, managing soil cultivation, irrigation, and plant protection, as well as implementing oenological strategies such as acid management.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Climate-resilient agriculture practices_qna_011
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What are the strategies for adapting to the changing climate in wine grape cultivation?
nodes.answer: Strategies for adapting to the changing climate in wine grape cultivation include switching to more heat and drought-resistant grape varieties, limiting damage by growing different varieties, and potentially benefitting from the warming climate by cultivating late-ripening varieties of cooler regions like Czechia.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Climate-resilient agriculture practices_qna_012
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How have colder regions like Germany adapted to climate change in their winemaking process?
nodes.answer: Colder regions like Germany have adapted to climate change by building irrigation systems in vineyards to combat the increase in evaporation due to rising temperatures.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Climate-resilient agriculture practices_qna_013
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What impact will climate change have on wine production in the Czech Republic?
nodes.answer: Climate change and warming trends will lead to an increase in red wine production in the Czech Republic, potentially requiring the importation of white wines from regions further north due to changing preferences.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Climate-resilient agriculture practices_qna_014
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How are farming systems in hot and dry regions expected to be impacted by environmental and climate change?
nodes.answer: Farming systems in hot and dry regions are expected to be most severely affected by environmental and climate change.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Climate-resilient agriculture practices_qna_015
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How has climate change impacted viticulture, and what potential adaptations are being considered?
nodes.answer: Climate change has impacted viticulture, and potential adaptations being considered to address it are discussed in the update.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Climate change adaptation strategies|Climate-resilient agriculture practices_qna_016
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What percentage of crop growing areas may need new varieties to adapt to changing environmental conditions according to climate modeling?
nodes.answer: Nearly 40% of crop growing areas might require new varieties better adapted to new environmental conditions to sustain crop production.
nodes.paragraph: The results of climate modeling suggest that nearly 40% of crop growing areas might require new varieties better adapted to new environmental conditions to sustain crop production [20, 21]. Leveraging the genetic diversity of multiple wild ances - tors of wheat, which evolved to grow in diverse environments, is one of the promising strategies for broadening the climate adaptive potential of modern wheat. The direct ancestors of wheat, Aegilops tauschii and Triticum turgidum ssp. dicoc - coides (wild emmer), are two most broadly distributed species among the wheat wild relatives [7, 10, 11, 13, 22, 23]. The signatures of extensive ancient introgression from these wild ancestors were detected across the wheat genome [17, 24, 25]. These ancient introgressions increased diversity genome-wide and contributed to environmental adap - tation [17]. Both Ae. tauschii and T. turgidum are also among the most represented in germplasm collections, some of which host thousands of accessions of these species [26]. Because these wild ancestors of wheat share homologous genomes, their chromosomes could easily recombine, facilitating introgression of allelic diversity from Ae.
